'''''Portulaca grandiflora''''' is a [[Succulent plant|succulent]] [[flowering plant]] in the purslane family [[Portulacaceae]], native to southern [[Brazil]], [[Argentina]], and [[Uruguay]] and often cultivated in gardens.<ref name=rhs>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref><ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 10 January 2018}}</ref> It has many [[common name]]s, including '''rose moss''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=POGR7|taxon=Portulaca grandiflora|accessdate=31 January 2016}}</ref> '''eleven o'clock''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''Mexican rose''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''moss rose''',<ref name=GRIN/>  '''sun rose''',<ref 
name=GRIN/>  '''rose Jepun''',<ref name=Mitchell>{{cite book |author=Mitchell, H. |year=2003  |title=The Essential Earthman: Henry Mitchell on Gardening |publisher=Indiana University Press |isbn=9780253215857 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O5fRmqDualkC |page=113}}</ref> '''table rose''',{{citation needed|date=September 2023}} '''rock rose''',<ref name=Mitchell/> and '''moss-rose [[purslane]]'''. Despite these names and the superficial resemblance of some cultivars' flowers to [[rose]]s, it is not a true rose, nor even a part of the [[Rosaceae|rose family]] or [[Rosids|rosid]] group; rather, it is much more closely related to [[carnation]]s and [[cactus|cacti]].

It is also seen in South Asia and widely spread in most of the cities with old 18th- and 19th-century architecture in the [[Balkans]].

==Description==
It is a small, but fast-growing [[annual plant]] growing to 30 cm tall, though usually less. However, if it is cultivated properly, it can easily reach this height. The [[leaf|leaves]] are thick and fleshy, up to 2.5 cm long, arranged alternately or in small clusters. The [[flower]]s are 2.5–3 cm diameter with five petals, variably red, orange, pink, white, and yellow.<ref name=rhs/> Their upright, or ascending, long shoots branch usually near the base. The spreading 20-to-25-millimeters-long and 2-to-3-millimeters-wide leaves are almost or completely stalk-shaped, and taper towards the tip.

The [[Axillary (botany)|axillary]] leaves have few to numerous whitish, woolly hairs which are usually shorter than the sheets. The compressed [[inflorescence]]s are surrounded by eight to ten leaves. The large flowers reach a diameter of up to 4 centimetres. The five bright [[magenta]]-coloured petals are [[obovate]] and 15 to 26 millimeters long. Around the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] with four to nine whitish scars are about 50 [[stamens]]. [[Capsule (fruit)|Capsule]]s and [[seed]]s are not visible.<ref>Urs Eggli (ed.): Succulent Encyclopedia. Dicots (dicotyledons). Eugen Ulmer, Stuttgart 2001, {{ISBN|3-8001-3662-7}}, pp.  437-438 .</ref>

''P. grandiflora'' is one of the few plants that is a {{c4}}/CAM intermediate, utilizing both [[C4 carbon fixation|{{c4}} carbon fixation]] and [[Crassulacean acid metabolism]] pathways in different cells for photosynthesis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guralnick|first1=Lonnie|last2=Gilbert|first2=Kate|last3=Denio|first3=Diana|last4=Antico|first4=Nicholas|date=2020-01-01|title=The Development of Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM) Photosynthesis in Cotyledons of the C4 Species, Portulaca grandiflora (Portulacaceae)|url=https://docs.rwu.edu/fcas_fp/401|journal= Plants|volume=9|issue=1|page=55|doi=10.3390/plants9010055|pmid=31906418|pmc=7020464|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been selected for double flowers with additional petals, and for variation in flower colour, plain or variegated.<ref name=rhs/> It is widely grown in temperate climates as an [[ornamental plant]] for annual bedding or as a container plant. It requires ample sunlight and well-drained soils. It requires almost no attention and spreads itself very easily. In places with old architecture it can grow between the stones of the road or sidewalk. Seeds are often sold as mixtures, such as ''Double Flowering Mixture'' (see illustrations). It grows on sandy soils. In countries with a frost-free climate, it is wild.<ref>Blumea. Tijdschrift voor de Systematiek en Geography of the Plants. Volume 17, No. 2, p. 297, Leiden 1969</ref><ref>Botanical Magazine; or, Flower-Garden Displayed. Volume 56, Plate 2885. London 1829</ref>

Unlike ''[[Portulaca oleracea|P. oleracea]]'' and ''[[Portulaca umbraticola|P. umbraticola]]'', it is not edible because of its bitter taste. There are hybrids of ''P. grandiflora'' with ''P. oleracea'', ''umbraticola'' and ''villosa''.

It is visited by [[Honey bee|honeybees]] for its [[pollen]] and [[nectar]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.florabeilles.org/serie/portulaca-grandiflora_apis-mellifera|title=Portulaca grandiflora & Apis mellifera|date=2012-09-09|website=Florabeilles|language=fr|access-date=2019-07-08}}</ref>
